units.text: Accelerated fabrication of antibacterial and osteoinductive electrospun fibrous scaffolds via electrochemical deposition †
Introduction

Electrospun bers resemble the natural extracellular matrix (ECM); their structural similarities allow the engineering of an ideal bionic environment for cell adhesion and reproduction, thus promoting the growth of new tissues. At present, electrospun brous scaffolds have many applications in orthopedics and other relevant elds. 1 However, because the main body of electrospun bers is predominantly polymer based, orthopedic applications are limited by poor surface bioactivity, which remains a great challenge for researchers. On the other hand, hydroxyapatite (HA), the main inorganic component of most naturally occurring calcied tissues in humans, is currently considered an optimal material for osteoinduction due to its high bioactivity. 2 He et al. 3 showed that an HA coating on the surface of poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) bers promoted the deposition of calcium and phosphorus ions in a physiological environment; thus, it facilitated the adhesion and reproduction of osteocytes, as well as osteoblastic differentiation. As a result, HA was able to accelerate the integration between the implant and its surrounding tissues, forming a uniform identity. 3 Therefore, the fabrication of electrospun brous scaffolds with HA coatings have the potential to signicantly increase the bioactivity and biocompatibility of implant materials.

At present, the most commonly used method for coating HA on electrospun bers is liquid immersion. 4 Hu et al. used an electrospinning method to make HA micro-nanoparticle composite PLLA brous scaffolds. 5 The HA composite material was able to provide nucleation sites for calcium phosphate in an in vitro immersion experiment; thus, it increased the bioactivity of the brous scaffold, forming an enriched layer of Ca-P at the ber surfaces. However, in the process of integrating HA micro-nanoparticles into the brous scaffold, HA was oen observed to agglomerate due to the separation of organic and inorganic phases. As a result, the mechanical properties of the material were signicantly compromised. In vivo, the addition of regulating agents, such as cell growth factors, amino acids etc., can increase the deposition and growth efficiencies of calcium phosphate. 6 Guo et al. biomineralized PLLA/gelatin nanobers in an amino-acid-rich articial body uid and found that the presence of amino acids increased the preferential growth of HA crystals along the c axis, promoting the formation of HA acicular crystals. 7 However, in vitro bio-mineralization in simulated body uid (SBF) needs at least several weeks for the desirable outcomes, and long immersion times can lead to drug release and material degradation. [8][9][10] Therefore, an efficient deposition method for calcied HA bioactive coatings on brous scaffold surfaces remains a challenge and an urgent issue that needs to be solved.

Pulsed electrodeposition (ED) is an important technique used to control the rate of a reaction. When the pulsed signals are applied, the electrolyte inside the electro-bath alternates the charging and discharging processes. The intermittent nature of the reaction at the electrode favors the diffusion process and it mitigates the risk of concentration polarization. In this way, the efficiency of deposition can be greatly improved. 11 Hence, the pairing of pulsed ED and electrospinning techniques has the potential to construct brous scaffolds on a calcium phosphate composite surface at a relatively fast speed. Due to the electric eld inside the pulsed ED solution, brous membranes are able to maintain a state of supersaturation of calcium and phosphate ions at micro-reactional regions of the cathode. The ions and electrospun bers have high specic surface areas; the resulting molecular interactions give rise to the fast nucleation and growth processes of calcium phosphate crystals. 12 In addition, because ED takes place in a solution, it is possible to achieve a porous brous scaffold or matrix with a uniformly distributed calcium phosphate coating; it is also possible to precisely control the morphology and size of the calcium phosphate crystals by adjusting the electrochemical parameters. Therefore, ED is a promising method for increasing the degree of mineralization while at the same time decreasing the mineralization time at surfaces of the material; it thereby accelerates the HA coating process at brous surfaces. However, an electrospun scaffold made of degradable PLLA has poor conductivity; consequently, it is difficult for rapid calcium phosphate deposition to take place directly in the electrolyte during ED.

To further improve the ED efficiency at composite surfaces, metals with high conductivity, such as Cu, Ni and nano-Ag are used as co-electrospinning dopants. [13][14][15] Surfaces of Cu and Ni nanoparticles are prone to oxidation as their elemental forms are unstable. 16 In comparison, nano-Ag has high specic conductance and is chemically stable; hence it has received much research interest as an antibacterial agent in medicallyrelated elds. 17 Nano-Ag in PLLA bers will enhance the conductive properties of the composite scaffold, thereby accelerating the mineralization process of calcium phosphate coatings and signicantly increasing the efficiency of scaffold fabrication; the composite scaffold product will also inherit the antibacterial and bioactivity properties from nano-Ag.

The structure of our PLLA/nano-Ag composite brous scaffold and the ED mineralization process taking place at the surfaces are illustrated in Scheme 1. This study reports a composite brous scaffold fabricated by electrospinning which has the majority of highly conductive nano-Ag distributed uniformly at the ber surfaces. In the process of ED, ber conductivity was observed to increase due to the nano-Ag dopant; upon applying the pulse signals when charging, water electrolysis occurred at micro-reactive regions of anodic bers, forming OH À , an alkaline environment that supported the supersaturation of calcium phosphate. When discharging, calcium phosphate in the solution diffused rapidly and reduced the concentration polarization, reforming a homogeneous electrolyte. The realization of efficient bioactive coatings at ber surfaces was quickly achieved by repeating the charging and discharging processes. The paper systematically investigated the morphologies of the calcium phosphate particles deposited at ber surfaces at various electrolyte concentrations, 42 mmol L À1 , 16.7 mmol L À1 and 5 mmol L À1 . Using SEM, it was observed that calcium phosphate deposition at ber surfaces appeared to be well-dispersed and the particles appeared to be ner when the ED electrolyte concentration was 16.7 mmol L À1 (Fig. S1 †).
Materials and methods
Materials

Chemicals were obtained from the following suppliers: poly(Llactic acid) (PLLA) from Jinan Daigang Biomaterial Co., Ltd; nano-Ag (diameter < 100 nm) from Sigma-Aldrich; dichloromethane (DCM) from Tianjin Yongsheng Fine Chemicals Co., Ltd; N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF) from Tianjin no. 3 Chemical Reagent Factory; calcium nitrate tetrahydrate (Ca(NO 3 ) 2 -$4H 2 O) from Tianjin Zhiyuan Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd; and ammonium dihydrogen phosphate (NH 4 H 2 PO 4 ) from Tianjin Shengao Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.
Instruments

A thin layer of gold was sprayed on top of each ber composite sample to increase its surface conductivity, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM; SU8010, Japan) was used to capture its morphology. Soware Image was used for dimensional analyses such as the average size and distribution of bers. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEM-2100F, Japan) was used to capture the morphology of nano-Ag alone and in PLLA. Thermogravimetric (TG) analysis (TGA-DSA 2960 TA instruments) was conducted to determine the nano-Ag content in the ber composite samples. A heating rate of 10 C min À1 from 10 to 800 C was used to measure the heat properties of the ber samples in a nitrogen environment.
Electrospinning solution

Nano-Ag solutions (3 wt%, 5 wt% and 7 wt%) were prepared in DMF; the mixtures were stirred thoroughly, and sonicated. PLLA solutions (10 wt%, 12 wt%, 14 wt% and 16 wt%) were prepared in DCM : DMF solution (2 : 1, wt%) and stirred thoroughly. Nano-Ag and PLLA mixtures were blended together and the resulting solutions were used for electrospinning.
Experimental procedures

A 20 mL plastic syringe with a no. 6 medical stainless-steel needle head was lled with electrospinning solution. The electrospun bers were collected 15 cm from the needle tip, with the sample release rate set at a constant 3 mL h À1 and an electric eld of 18 kV cm À1 from a DC source. At the end of the process, electrospun bers were collected on an electrode collector or a tin foil (20 cm Â 13 cm Â 0.2 cm) wrapped around the spinning core. During electrolytic deposition, the nanobers were collected on a 200-300 mm-thick polar plate. When simulating the articial body uid environment, the nanobers collected on the tin foil were modied to have the same thickness as that obtained from ED.
Electrodeposition

Under constant voltage, the platinum (20 mm Â 20 mm Â 0.2 mm) and stainless-steel ber plates were set to opposite polarities, with the platinum plate functioning as the counter electrode and the stainless-steel ber plates functioning as the working electrodes. The two electrodes were set 2.5 cm apart and the electrochemical beaker (250 mL) was bathed to maintain a specic temperature. The electrolyte was a mixture of 16.7 mmol L À1 Ca(NO 3 ) 2 $4H 2 O and 10 mmol L À1 NH 4 H 2 PO 4 . Based on results from ED, the mineralized PLLA was retrieved from the stainless-steel electrode, dried naturally and characterized.
Humoral mineralization stimulation

The ber composite from supersaturated calcium phosphate solution (SCPS) was mineralized in vitro. The sample product was tailored into a 20 mm Â 20 mm square and le immersed in 40 mL SCPS at 37 C, with the solution changed every 24 h. The ionic concentration of the solution was set to match that in blood (Table S1 †) and Tris-HCl was used as a buffer with the pH set to 6.2-6.3 at room temperature. When the sample was retrieved, it was washed with deionized (DI) water and kept at 37 C in a vacuum drying oven.
Ion release tests

The composite coating was soaked in a 40 mL phosphate solution (PBS, pH ¼ 7.4) at 37 C for 10 days and the release proles of Ca 2+ and Ag + were recorded. Atomic absorption spectrophotometry was used to determine the absorbance values of Ca 2+ and Ag + ; their respective concentrations were determined from standard curves, and values were used to investigate the physiological instability of the composite coating layer (Table S2 †).
Antibacterial capability

Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus were selected for both qualitative and quantitative analyses, and experiments were performed with three groups: PLLA/nano-Ag, ED, and SCPS, each with three parallel samples. The spread plate method was used for qualitative analysis and the lm adhering method was used for quantitative analysis.
Qualitative analysis

Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus were cultured on LB medium at 37 C for 12 h, and then a moderate amount of each was picked by inoculation loop and cultured in a uid nutrient medium for 12 h to obtain a bacterial suspension solution. Next, 10 mL 1 Â 10 8 cell per mL suspension solutions were made from each of Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus using PBS. The samples were le at 37 C in a 200 rpm swing bed for 12 h. In the end, 100 mL of each was obtained for the corresponding spread plate, which was kept in an incubator at 37 C for 12 h; colonies were recorded and photographed.
Quantitative analysis

The antibacterial rate was investigated with the lm adhering method. Both bacterial strains were cultured in LB medium at 37 C for 12 h and the process was repeated three times to obtain purer colonies. A colony was inoculated to a uid nutrient medium kept at 37 C, in a 200 rpm swing bed for 12 h. Solutions (3.0 Â 10 7 cell per mL) were made using PBS, and diluted 10 3 -fold. Each sample to be measured was placed on a slide and sterile water was added to the bottom of the Petri dish to prevent evaporation. A 50 mL droplet was added to the sample surface and cultured at 37 C for 24 h; then the bacterial solution was blended with the PBS solution, shaken well, smeared onto the spread plate, kept for 24 h and counted for the number of colonies. The antibacterial capabilities of the samples were calculated using the formula shown below. PLLA/ nano-Ag was used as the control group; experiments for three parallel samples were conducted in each case and an average bacterial ratio was calculated.
Antibacterial rate ¼ CCCG À CCEG CCCG Â 100%

where CCCG is the colony count of the control group and CCEG is the colony count of the experimental group. The samples were placed into six-well culture dishes and MC3T3-E1 cells were inoculated onto the sample surfaces with an inoculum density of 7.5 Â 10 3 $mL À1 . L-DMEME nutrient medium (3.0 mL) was added to each well and samples were kept in a CO 2 incubator at 37 C and treated as follows: (1) aer 1, 3, 5, 7 days, samples from each of the three groups were washed three times using PBS and sealed twice by serum, each for 30 min; then 2.5% glutaraldehyde solution was used for immobilization, and gradient ethanol solution was used for dealcoholization. Aer the dried samples were plated with thin layers of gold for conductivity, SEM was used to capture the morphologies of the cells.

(2) Aer 1, 3, 5, 7 days, cell proliferation and viability were determined by CCK-8 assay. Cell suspensions were inoculated onto a 96-well culture dish with 100 mL in each well and three parallel samples for each case. Upon adding 10 mL of CCK-8, the samples were kept in a CO 2 incubator at 37 C for 3 h and photometric absorption values at 450 nm were measured.
Statistical analysis

All data are presented as means AE standard deviation. Statistical analysis was carried out using a One Sample t test (assuming unequal variance). The difference between two sets of data was considered statistically signicant when P < 0.05.
Results and discussion

As shown in Fig. 1, PLLA bers had a smooth surface ( Fig. 1a and b) while PLLA/nano-Ag composite bers were evenly distributed and their surfaces were covered by nano-Ag particles ( Fig. 1d and e). The diameters of the nano-Ag particles were smaller than 100 nm and the bers completely encapsulated the particles (Fig. 1c). The PLLA and PLLA/nano-Ag water contact angles were found to be 132.2 and 139.1 respectively through contact angle measurements ( Fig. 1a and d). Because nano-Ag dopant increased the roughness of the ber surfaces, PLLA/ nano-Ag bers displayed more hydrophobicity than PLLA bers. 18 The aforementioned structures also allowed the composite to slowly release the nano-Ag dopant, achieving a long-term antibacterial effect. An experiment was conducted to investigate the quantity and consistency of Ag + release; it found that the Ag + level stayed constant at 1.0 ppm in the composite bers for the rst 10 days (Fig. 1f), indicating a desirable trait of steady release and showing that nano-Ag can be used as a continuous antibacterial dopant in PLLA.

To optimize the physical properties of the composite brous scaffold, the processing parameters of the electrospun PLLA/ nano-Ag composite brous scaffold were systematically explored. Shown in Fig. S2 † are the diameter proles and ber morphologies of PLLA fabricated at different concentrations. When the concentration was relatively low (10%, 12%), the average diameters of the bers were 300 nm and 370 nm; the bers were unevenly distributed and there were observable beads. The presence of beads could be attributed to the nonuniformity of the bers as a result of low surface tension due to low PLLA concentration. As the concentration increased (14%, 16%), the average diameters were observed to increase to 930 nm and 1040 nm. The bers were evenly distributed because the solution viscosity increased the surface tension, which became too great for the electric eld forces to overcome; thus, the average diameters increased accordingly. 19 Therefore, concentrations of PLLA of between 14% and 16% should be selected for superior performances. Fig. S3 † shows the morphology, diameter distribution and TG graph of bers fabricated at various nano-Ag concentrations. When the concentration of nano-Ag was lower than 3%, no adhesion was observed among bers and the overall ber thickness was even; the average diameter of the bers was 724 nm. When the concentration of nano-Ag was 5%, the composite bers were uniform and the average diameter was 893 nm (Fig. 1d). When the concentration of nano-Ag was 7%, a small proportion of bers started to agglomerate and the average diameter was 768 nm. The aggregation could be attributed to the fact that when the concentration was high, nano-Ag introduced discontinuities into the ber chains by occupying spaces among nanoparticles, thus lowering the tenacity of the bers. 20 As the concentration of nano-Ag increased, the amount of residual nano-Ag increased as well. For concentrations of 3%, 5% and 7% discussed above, the corresponding residuals were 2.03%, 4.64% and 4.89%. Therefore, composite bers should be optimal when the concentration of nano-Ag is from 3% to 5%.

Bioactivity is a main criterion for the effectiveness of integration at the interface of bone repairing materials and human bones. Mineralization can enhance the bioactivity of a material, promote osteoblast activity and facilitate osteogenesis. 21 Fig. S4 † shows the mineralization conditions at PLLA ber surfaces. Fig. S4a † illustrates that, in the ED mineralization process, when the average ber diameter was 930 nm, the quantity of calcium phosphate calcication was proportional to deposition time. Because pores existed among the PLLA bers that covered the stainless-steel surfaces, the calcium ions in the solution migrated towards the cathode under the effect of an electric eld. When the average ber diameter increased to 1040 nm, the quantity of calcium phosphate calcication was initially proportional but then inversely proportional to deposition time. One plausible explanation could be that the thicker bers had decreased pore sizes, which in turn reduced eld stress. In the process of deposition (35 min), as the ber diameter increased, the increasing amount of calcied calcium phosphate offered a greater surface area. Aer 35 min, potentially due to the lengthy electrolysis time, the calcium phosphate coating thickened, which in turn lowered the ber porosity, As a consequence, the hydrogen produced from the electrolysis reaction could not vent properly, causing the shedding of some calcium phosphate salt. The most commonly used way to determine the bioactivity of a material is by in vivo immersion in an SBF environment; the product of this method, apatite, integrates easily with bioactive bones. 22 Our research compares ED to in vivo immersion. Fig. S4b † presents pictures of calcied SCPS and shows that quantities of calcium phosphate calcication were inversely proportional to ber diameters. Since the nucleation sites for calcium and phosphate ions were the same, bers with smaller diameters offered greater specic surface areas which resulted in greater quantities of calcium phosphate calcication. 3 To conclude, calcium phosphate crystals grow faster and calcify more easily when the calcium phosphate is in a hyper-saturated state sustained by electric elds in ED.

The quantity of calcium phosphate calcication is a function of the nano-Ag content in composite bers. Fig. S5a † illustrates the mineralization by ED: when the nano-Ag content was low (#4.64%), the quantity of calcium phosphate mineralization at ber surfaces was proportional to the deposition time. As the nano-Ag content increased, the tendency for calcium phosphate to calcify increased as well. This was the case because nano-Ag increased the conductivity of the material, which was benecial for the deposition of calcium phosphate. 23 When the nano-Ag content increased to 4.89%, the calcication quantity initially increased but then dropped. This was because the thickening of the mineralization layer resulted in a decrease in the degree of porosity, which caused the conductivity to drop, making hydrogen gases produced in the electrolysis hard to vent. 24 In the meantime, bers with greater diameters (D Ag 2.03% < D Ag 4.89% < D Ag 4.64% ) provided greater surface areas, which promoted the deposition of calcium phosphate. Fig. S5b † illustrates the mineralization of SCPS and shows that there is no correlation between the quantity of calcium phosphate calcication at ber surfaces and the nano-Ag content added. As previously discussed, ber diameters were closely related to the quantity of calcium phosphate mineralization at ber surfaces. The smaller the diameter, the greater the specic surface area, which resulted in a greater quantity of calcium phosphate deposition at ber surfaces. Both mineralization methods, ED and SCPS, can therefore improve the bioactivity but the mineralization time needed differs signicantly. The ED mineralization method took 1 hour or less. Furthermore, the morphology, size and crystallinity could be modied by changing the processing parameters such as the temperature of the electrolyte, the electrical potential and deposition time. 25 In comparison, SCPS mineralization took longer to nish and it is worth noting that prolonged immersion could trigger drug release and lead to material degradation. 26 Fig. S6 † displays a collection of ber topographies resulting from both ED and SCPS calcication methods. Fig. S6a and b † show topographies of calcium phosphate depositions at PLLA ber surfaces before and aer the addition of nano-Ag using ED. Before adding nano-Ag, the calcium phosphate coating at the PLLA ber surface appeared to be acicular with low crystallinity. Aer adding nano-Ag, the calcium phosphate coating at the PLLA ber surface appeared to be ake-like and well-distributed with high crystallinity. The changes in topography could be explained by the fact that the nano-Ag distributed at the ber surface increased the electric current density at the ber surface. 27 Consequently, calcium phosphate was able to deposit at ber surfaces at electrochemically higher reaction rates. Fig. S6c and d † show topographies of calcium phosphate depositions at PLLA ber surfaces before and aer the addition of nano-Ag using SCPS. Aer the addition of nano-Ag, which increased the bioactivity of the PPLA bers, calcium phosphate deposition sites at the PLLA ber surfaces appeared to be akelike and globular; this could be the result of increasing nucleation sites at the PLLA surfaces due to the nano-Ag. Before the addition of nano-Ag, the calcium phosphate deposition at the PLLA ber surface was negligible. Thus, it is concluded that nano-Ag can promote in vitro bio-mineralization of PLLA ber surfaces.

To analyze the inuence of ED and SCPS bio-mineralization methods on the growth and evolution process of calcium phosphate at PLLA/nano-Ag composite ber surfaces, the conditions of calcium phosphate at various deposition times were recorded. Fig. 2 provides observations of the morphologies at 15, 30 and 60 minutes during the ED process. The calcium phosphate depositions at the composite ber surfaces appeared to be nanoparticles at 15 min (Fig. 2a). The nano-structures are closely related to deposition time; Eliaz et al. reported 3D growth of calcium monophosphide on titanium aer instantaneous nucleation, 2D continuous nucleation and ED (approximately 12 min). 28 Zhang et al. reported on a coating that initially formed an octacalcium phosphate layer, which also functioned as the precursor for HA. 29 The high pH value near the cathode was the driving force for transformation. As shown in Fig. 2b and a uniform layer of aky calcium phosphate rst formed at the ber surfaces. Then the calcium phosphate at the ber surfaces showed an inhomogeneous tendency at 60 min (Fig. 2c) because lengthy electrolysis times produce an excessively thick coating, blocking hydrogen gases from the electrolysis reaction from venting promptly. 24 According to the biomineralization mechanism outlined in Fig. 2d, pores existed among bers and positive ions migrated towards the cathode under the electric eld; water electrolysis took place at the cathode, producing hydrogen gases and hydroxyl groups; and the calcium phosphate near the composite bers reached a hyper-saturated state in the alkaline environment at the cathode. In addition, micro-reactions of bers took place in the alkaline environment; some PLLA reacted with water during ED and formed activated carboxyl groups. Activated carboxyl groups were susceptible to nucleation reactions with calcium ions and calcium phosphate, realizing the rapid growth of the calcium phosphate crystals. 30 Fig. S7 † shows the bio-mineralized calcium phosphate growth process for bers immersed in SCPS. No marked change was observed at the ber surfaces on day 3, but nanoparticles started to be scattered on the ber surfaces on day 7 and the structure of the nanoparticles was believed to be closely related Paper to the deposition time. 31 On day 12, akes of bio-mineralized sediments began to form at the ber surfaces. 32 Based on the observations above, the deposition mechanism can be divided into three stages: (1) during the dissolution phase, the ber surfaces interact with SCPS; some bers are hydrolyzed, producing active carboxyl functional groups. (2) During the Fig. 3 Antibacterial effects of the composite fibers. Fig. 4 ALP activity of osteoblasts cultured on different nano-fibrous matrices after 1, 3, 5 and 7 days in culture. Data are expressed as mean AE SD (n ¼ 3). A significant difference between groups is indicated by *(P < 0.05 compared with the neat PLLA/nano-Ag matrix) and **(the value of P for ED, SCPS and neat PLLA/nano-Ag matrix). deposition phase, negative ions at the ber surfaces attract and form an enriched layer of calcium ions from SCPS. (3) During the salt formation phase, the enriched layer of calcium ions attracts phosphate groups, resulting in the calcium phosphate coating. 33 Studies have shown that the bio-mineralization period of SCPS is longer than that of ED, for an equal amount of bio-mineralization. Further, the morphology of calcium phosphate can be changed to accelerate the bio-mineralization process of the calcium phosphate coating by simply adjusting the reaction parameters in ED. In this article, the experiments below were carried out with an ED bio-mineralization period set to 60 minutes.

As shown in Fig. 3, aer 12 hours of incubation at constant temperature, Escherichia coli colonies piled up to create a lawn of bacteria at the ber surface of the PLLA/nano-Ag control group, and on top of it there was a layer of viscous and pasty substances, visible to the naked eye, indicating strong metabolism of the bacteria. Only a small number of Staphylococcus aureus colonies were observed on the control ber surface while no distinct colonies were marked on the ED or SCPS surfaces signifying their strong antibacterial abilities. Results from a quantitative analysis regarding antibacterial capabilities showed the antibacterial ratio of the PLLA/nano-Ag bers to Escherichia coli to be 10% and the antibacterial ratio of the PLLA/nano-Ag bers to Staphylococcus aureus to be 95%; this agreed with data from Zhang et al. 34 ED and SCPS surfaces showed an antibacterial ratio of 99.5% and above against Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus. These high ratios could be explained by the fact that the space between akes of calcium phosphate facilitated nano-Ag release; in addition, the sharp edges of the calcium phosphate akes could damage the bacterial cell membranes. 35 Experimental outcomes from both quantitative and qualitative analyses showed that ED and SCPS had strong antibacterial activities.

Nano-Ag is able to enhance the antibacterial activity of composite bers signicantly. The primary mechanisms behind the antibacterial activity are metal-ion effects and photo-catalysis. 36,37 The chemical structure of Ag bestows strong catalytic ability; in addition, Ag has a high reduction potential, thus it can produce atomic oxygen in its surrounding environment. Atomic oxygen is a strong oxidizing agent, which is ideal for sterilization purposes. Further, an Ag + ion can pull itself towards the thiol groups on bacterial proteases, and then deactivate the proteases, causing the eventual death of the bacteria. Finally, the Ag + ion can migrate away from the dead bacteria and repeat the cycle stated above again and again. That is the reason for the remarkable sustainability of the antibacterial activity of Ag. Fig. 4 shows different morphologies of osteocytes cultured at composite ber surfaces (ED 60 min, SCPS 12 days) during a seven-day period. From day 1 to day 3, adhesion started to take place at the ber surfaces; on day 5, osteocytes began to spread on the ber surfaces; and on day 7, osteocytes became well dispersed at the ber surfaces. The distribution at ED ber surfaces was particularly good, likely due to its higher degree of roughness. 38 Studies showed that ED bers facilitate cell adhesion and adequately maintain cellular morphology. Furthermore, alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity assays found no marked difference in the differentiation ability of osteocytes at the different surfaces on day 5. However, the differentiation ability of osteocytes at ED ber surfaces was signicantly higher than that at SCPS ber surfaces on day 7; and the differentiation abilities of both ED and SCPS ber surfaces were higher than that of a surface without calcium phosphate. In addition, 5% Ag had no impact on osteoblasts, while the ED ber surface was shown to have strong capability to induce osteogenic differentiation. In conclusion, this paper has reported a pulsed ED method that can accelerate the bio-mineralization process of Ag-doped ber surfaces, forming an antibacterial brous scaffold with high bioactivity and strong osteogenesis capability.
Conclusions

Herein we have presented a method for fabricating PLLA/nano-Ag composite bers that facilitates the growth of calcium phosphate crystals at the ber surfaces and promotes osteogenic differentiation, thus signicantly improving the fabrication efficiency of osteoinductive electrospun bers. The study found the ber diameter to be proportional to the PLLA concentration and the optimized concentration to be 14%. The ber diameters were observed to be even when the concentration of nano-Ag was relatively low and the morphology showed the highest degree of homogeneity when the concentration of Ag was between 3% and 5%. The release rate of Ag + ions in composite bers was highly stable and remained at 1.0 ppm per day for 10 days. ED was utilized to accelerate the biomineralization process of calcium phosphate, and comparisons to traditional SCPS were made and analyzed. The quantity of bio-mineralized calcium phosphate at ber surfaces was directly proportion to the deposition time and closely related to the ber diameter as well as to the nano-Ag concentration; in an ED process, when the concentration of nano-Ag was 5%, the larger the ber diameter, the greater the amount of calcium phosphate deposited, and the shorter the bio-mineralization process. Experimentally, the ED composite also demonstrated strong antibacterial properties and the capability to induce osteoblast differentiation at ber surfaces. Therefore, ED can be adopted to simplify and accelerate the fabrication process of an osteogenetic and antibacterial electrospun brous scaffold.
